findings.title: "NumPy is the only backend that exists today" is false; the `numpy` row would measure Numba kernels
findings.description:
Slice 118 (Numba Force JIT) is `status: complete`, and its design states the JIT flag's "default in production code is `True`". Slice 140 describes the substrate as "NumPy today, Numba already". This design's own workload comment says the warmup "lets caches/JIT warm" (line 388).

The `numpy` backend is specified as "today's `engine.tick.tick`" driving the existing `BulkForce` implementations, with no mention of the JIT flag. Consequences:

- **Mislabelled baseline.** `force_total` under `backend: "numpy"` is Numba time, and the "NumPy golden" parity hash (lines 465-467) comes from the JIT path.
- **Gap for slice 142.** The plan says "Numba and Quadrants slot in as those backends become available", and Numba is available now. Deferring the Numba runner to "slice 144 / 118 territory" (line 92) leaves nobody delivering it before 142, which depends on (141) and (118) and must compare Quadrants against both.
- **Corrupted gate.** Slice 142's go/no-go ("under what conditions does Quadrants beat Numba?") would rest on a mislabelled baseline.

Required changes:

1. The `numpy` runner explicitly pins the engine JIT flag off.
2. A `numba` runner is registered in this slice; by the design's own claim (lines 341-345) it is one file.
3. The JIT setting is recorded in the JSON report.
4. Because the flag is process-global, state how `--all-backends` sets and restores it per runner. This also answers the subprocess-isolation open question for the CPU pair.

findings.title: Per-force timing is assigned to this slice by the plan but deferred to 142
findings.description:
The slice plan entry for 141 specifies phases as "spatial build, spatial query, CSR assembly, **force totals per force**, integration". The design collapses this to one `force_total_ns` and hands per-force resolution to slice 142.

- **Internal contradiction.** The integration criterion says 142 adds a backend with "zero changes elsewhere in the harness" (lines 586-588), yet 142 would have to extend `PhaseTimings`, both renderers and bump `schema_version`.
- **Cheap to do now.** The force phase is already a loop over the force list, so bracketing each iteration is trivial in `tick_instrumented`.
- **Fix.** Ship `force_breakdown` in schema v1 and keep `force_total` as the sum.

The same rigidity will hit slice 145: `PhaseTimings` requires all five CPU-shaped phases as mandatory ints, but a fused GPU tick has no separate `csr_assembly`. Say whether an inapplicable phase is omitted or null, not silently zero.

findings.title: Parity hash cannot serve the cross-backend role the design assigns it
findings.description:
The design says slice 145's tick-level parity test "consumes the harness's NumPy parity hash as the reference" (lines 533-534), and that downstream consumers interpret a GPU hash "within the documented tolerance band".

- **A hash has no tolerance.** A SHA-256 of raw bytes is either equal or not.
- **The plan requires tolerance.** Slice 145's entry asks for parity "within a documented tolerance", and slice 118's criterion is `np.allclose(atol=1e-12)`, so even Numba is not promised bit-identical to NumPy.
- **Divergence is certain.** After 660 ticks of a chaotic flocking system, any non-bit-exact backend will produce a different hash, so the field always reads "different".

Either scope the hash to what it can do (same-backend, same-platform determinism and regression detection) and remove the 145 integration claim, or persist the final arrays so a tolerance comparison is possible. The Open Questions already name `tools/run_deterministic_trajectory.py` as the parity oracle, so the first option is the lighter one.

Separately, the data flow calls `finalize()` (which releases GPU memory) before `parity.hash(result)` at lines 205-211. Slice 140's lifetime rule on `TickResult` means the hash must be taken before teardown.

findings.title: Consumed interfaces are described inconsistently and partly do not match the providing documents
findings.description:
- **`tick()` call contradiction.** Lines 131-132 and 541 say the NumPy runner "calls `tick()` directly". Decision B (lines 255-267) says it runs a re-implemented `tick_instrumented()` and never calls `tick()`.
- **Unlisted internals.** The re-implementation needs the self-exclusion and neighbour-cap helpers, the CSR container, the integrator and the density-notification hook. None appear under Interfaces Required.
- **"~5 lines per phase" understates the copy.** It is the whole tick body, including both query paths (k-capped fast path and radius plus cap).
- **Spatial module named two ways.** It is `migratory.spatial` at line 136 and `engine.spatial.KDTreeQuery` at line 542.
- **Spatial backend not recorded.** It is neither a workload field nor a report field, although the plan makes it "per-tier, config-selectable" and slice 143 compares backends through this harness.
- **Force singletons.** Force names "resolve to module-level singleton instances (e.g. `flocking.cohesion_force`)" (lines 398-400). Slice 118 describes forces as classes assembled by `build_forces()`. Name the real construction path and reuse it, or the harness duplicates engine wiring.
- **Profile presets.** Profile names resolve to "`migratory.engine.profile` presets" or "constructors used in `config/default.yaml`" (lines 392-396). Profiles there are inline parameter blocks, and no `flocker` or `leader` preset is defined. The harness therefore must invent profile parameters, contradicting "does not invent new profiles". Put the parameters in the workload YAML.
- **Propulsion omitted.** The plan's slice 144 entry lists six `BulkForce`s including `PropulsionForce`; the design says "the five existing". A `mid-flock` workload without propulsion is not "roughly equivalent to the live-server default" (lines 353-355).

findings.title: Headline metrics and report aggregation are under-specified
findings.description:
- **`tps_observed` has no definition.** In the sample, 600 ticks / 9.21 s gives 65.1, while mean `total_ns` of 9.55 ms implies about 105 TPS. `wall_seconds` evidently includes setup or warmup, which makes TPS incomparable across backends with different setup or compile cost. Define it from the measured window only.
- **Statistics method unstated.** State the percentile method and stdev convention so the "stable" v1 schema is reproducible.
- **Markdown source set unclear.** Line 440 says the table spans "all backends in `bench/results/`", which means reading prior result files, while State Management says the harness is stateless. Say which files are selected, or render only the current invocation.
- **CLI flags missing from the CLI section.** `--list-backends` and `--list-workloads` appear only in the walkthrough.
- **`density` field missing.** It is listed as a workload field (line 71) and in the plan, but is absent from the schema.

findings.title: Failure-mode enumeration misses three of the new I/O paths
findings.description:
The four listed modes cover the loader, the registry, `setup` and low TPS. Unhandled:

- **`tick_once` raising mid-measure.** Is `finalize` called, and is a partial report written or suppressed?
- **`git rev-parse` subprocess.** Git absent or not a repo must be an explicit error, not an empty `git_sha`. A dirty tree stamps uncommitted code with HEAD's SHA, which breaks the "reproducible by repo hash" claim; add a dirty flag.
- **Result write.** `bench/results/` missing or unwritable after a ten-second run.
- **Hang.** No timeout is stated. "None; interrupt and `finalize` runs" is acceptable but must be written down before GPU backends arrive.
- **Loader validation beyond missing fields.** Malformed YAML, wrong types, and profile fractions that do not sum to 1.
- **`finalize` on a half-set-up runner.** `setup` raising calls `finalize` on a partially initialised runner; state that `finalize` must tolerate that.
- **Magic threshold.** "TPS < 1" should be a named constant.

findings.title: Drift mitigation does not cover the tick changes already planned
findings.description: The bit-equality test catches algorithmic drift only on the paths it exercises. Slice 119 adds an optional neighbour cache to `tick()` whose default is behaviour-neutral, so the copy would stay bit-equal while no longer timing the production path. The test should cover both query paths and `active_indices`. Decision B is acceptable for one caller; the stated "third call site" trigger for revisiting is reasonable.

findings.title: Small proportionality cuts and metadata additions
Layer boundaries and dependency direction
findings.description: The harness depends on the engine and never the reverse. It excludes the world server, websocket and logging layers, consistent with "the wire is a separate problem". It reads post-tick state only through `TickResult`, as slice 140's cross-slice interface section expects. Deferring NVIDIA runs, CI gating and memory measurement is consistent with the plan ("standalone against NumPy at first", "memory is not a roadmap constraint").

findings.title: NFR and architectural principle coverage
findings.description: The slice adds no code to the production tick path, so the 60 TPS target is unaffected. It restates the architecture's Entry 8 per-phase reference budget as the profile-shape check. The three workloads (`dispersed`, `mid-flock`, `packed-herd`) match the formation regimes the plan names for the Profile Principle, and JSON output satisfies the "CSV/JSON" machine-readable requirement.
